title: USB PD negotiation and current entitlement
summary: Require a valid supported PD contract before using negotiated voltage/current. Keep startup and fallback consumption within the permitted non-PD budget.
required_inputs: Source capabilities, sink demand, controller policy and cable capabilities
Supported PD revision, startup supply and allowed fallback
verification: Observe requested/accepted contracts and confirm actual VBUS and load behavior; test unsupported requests and renegotiation.
limitations: Rd alone cannot request 9/12/15/20 V. A generic PD trigger board does not prove safe fallback or sufficient cable capability.

citations.locator: USB Type-C DFP/UFP and DRP/DRD block diagrams; USB PD and SuperSpeed sections, pages 3-10 (historical edition)
Publisher release page and linked USB_PD_R3.2_V1.2(3).zip; edition identification only

title: USB PD controller and protected power-path pattern
summary: Coordinate PD policy with a suitably rated switch/converter/charger path. The negotiation controller alone does not establish regulation, thermal or protection performance.
applies_to: Power delivery circuits with explicit source/sink roles.
required_inputs: Contract envelope, power-stage topology and component ratings
Inrush, capacitance, reverse current, discharge and thermal budgets
verification: Verify startup, attach/detach, contract transitions, faults and board-off behavior.
Read back copper dimensions and check current, voltage drop and temperature under intended load.
limitations: No universal VBUS capacitor, fuse, TVS or MOSFET value applies. Review limits at the connector separately from bulk capacitance behind a switch.

citations.locator: SPR/EPR comparison and battery-powered system architecture; verify current PD requirements separately
IEC ESD and short-to-VBUS events, pages 3-10; historical 20 V examples are not EPR ratings

pattern.diagram:
CC1/CC2 <-> PD controller -> policy/status/control
Receptacle VBUS <-> protected power path <-> converter/charger/system
Direction follows the selected power role.
placement: Place local bypassing, switches and protection to control the relevant power loops.
routing: Route all required VBUS contacts and size neck-downs/vias for the selected envelope.
return_path: Keep high-current returns from sharing sensitive measurement impedance.
pitfalls: A buck/boost stage or battery charger may still be needed after negotiation.

title: USB PD SPR, EPR, PPS and AVS capability boundaries
summary: Select the required power range and supply features explicitly. EPR requires compatible controller, power path and cable; PPS and AVS are distinct capabilities.
applies_to: Capability planning for USB PD products, including EPR.
required_inputs: Controller revision/features, source profiles, cable rating and requested operating range
verification: Check capability advertisement and contract transitions with representative sources/cables, including unsupported combinations.
limitations: 100 W is not the current universal PD ceiling. Do not assume every PD port supports EPR, PPS or AVS, or import old application-note voltage/current tables as current normative limits.
